title: Does Goal-Setting Help or Harm Teacher Motivation?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart examines why goal-setting can either help or hurt a teacher's own motivation, arguing the deciding factor isn't goal-setting frameworks like SMART or WOOP but the teacher's current position on the Yerkes-Dodson pressure curve. For teachers who feel over-pressured, he recommends a "can't miss" goal entirely within their own control — like conducting a set number of pop-up debates or personal check-ins with students — because such goals are self-reinforcing and don't depend on student cooperation. Somewhat counterintuitively, he argues under-pressured teachers need the same kind of self-controlled goal rather than a "moonshot" goal like a target test score, since shared-control goals don't reliably restore motivation the way locus-of-control goals do. He closes with a practical caveat: the goal only works if the underlying activity is the kind that genuinely benefits from quantity and repetition, not busywork dressed up as a metric.
points: Stuart's central move is locating teacher-motivation goal-setting inside the Yerkes-Dodson pressure curve rather than treating it as a generic productivity technique.

His "can't miss" goal category — entirely within the teacher's own locus of control (debates held, connections made, mini-sermons given) — is explicitly designed to be self-reinforcing rather than dependent on external outcomes like test scores.

He challenges the intuitive fix for under-pressured teachers (set a harder, shared-control "moonshot" goal) and argues the same self-controlled goal type works better regardless of pressure direction.
The closing caveat — that tracked actions must be the kind that "benefit from quantity and repetition" — guards against teachers gaming the technique with goals that look productive but aren't.
quotes: Goal-setting: does it help or harm teacher motivation? This is an interesting problem to me.
However, the type of goal you set massively predicts whether it will help or hinder your motivation.
It posits, quite commonsensically, that a given human's performance hinges on that human experiencing an ideal degree of pressure — not too little and not too much.
I call these "can't miss" goals because whether or not I meet them is totally up to me and how I focus my time and energy. I am the locus of control.
But actually, I don't think this is the kind of goal that you need if you're under-pressured. I think you need the same kind of goal as you need when in the over-pressured condition.

But the important thing, of course, is that you make sure that the actions you're tracking — in my example above, it was debates and MGCs and mini-sermons — are actually things that benefit from quantity and repetition.
And as you go, observe what's happening in your heart. Are you becoming more motivated or less? Are you experiencing more pressure or less?
